retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III, point 4
retrieved_evidence.text: 4. Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III — High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
retrieved_evidence.text: ANNEX III High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) High-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) are the AI systems listed in any of the following areas: 1. Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) remote biometric identification systems. This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be; (b) AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation, according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics; (c) AI systems intended to be used for emotion recognition. 2. Critical infrastructure: AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. 3. Education and vocational training: (a) AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (c) AI systems intended to be used for the purpose of assessing the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (d) AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. 4. Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. 5. Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits: (a) AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud; (c) AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance; (d) AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems. 6. Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities or on their behalf to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities as polygraphs or similar tools; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in support of law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of the investigation or prosecution of criminal offences; (d) AI systems intended to be used by law enforcement authorities or on their behalf or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, or to assess personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups; (e) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 in the course of the detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. 7. Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies as polygraphs or similar tools; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assist competent public authorities for the examination of applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and for associated complaints with regard to the eligibility of the natural persons applying for a status, including related assessments of the reliability of evidence; (d) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in the context of migration, asylum or border control management, for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, with the exception of the verification of travel documents. 8. Administration of justice and democratic processes: (a) AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority or on their behalf to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used in a similar way in alternative dispute resolution; (b) AI systems intended to be used for influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda. This does not include AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

retrieved_evidence.label: Article 6 — Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems 1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; (b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. ▼M1 1a. For the purposes of this Regulation, including paragraph 1 of this Article, AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components. 1b. Notwithstanding paragraph 1a, AI systems the failure or malfunctioning of which would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components. 1c. A product that is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than risks to health and safety, in particular risks relating to the distribution of radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, shall not be considered as fulfilling the condition in paragraph 1, point (b). ▼B 2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. 3. By derogation from paragraph 2, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. The first subparagraph shall apply where any of the following conditions is fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III. Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons. 4. A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2). Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider shall provide the documentation of the assessment. 5. The Commission shall, after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board (the ‘Board’), and no later than 2 February 2026, provide guidelines specifying the practical implementation of this Article in line with Article 96 together with a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk. 6. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by adding new conditions to those laid down therein, or by modifying them, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of the existence of AI systems that fall under the scope of Annex III, but do not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. 7. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by deleting any of the conditions laid down therein, where there is concrete and reliable evidence that this is necessary to maintain the level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation. 8. Any amendment to the conditions laid down in paragraph 3, second subparagraph, adopted in accordance with paragraphs 6 and 7 of this Article shall not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation and shall ensure consistency with the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Article 7(1), and take account of market and technological developments.

retrieved_evidence.label: Article 113 — Entry into force and application
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 113 Entry into force and application This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: ▼M1 (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025, with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026; ▼B (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; ▼M1 (c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I; ▼M1 (d) Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026. ▼B

answer:
### Provisional finding

The system provisionally falls within the high-risk classification scope under Annex III, point 4 via Article 6(2). However, whether the system is ultimately classified as high-risk depends on unresolved material facts: specifically, whether the automated filtering and ranking materially influence decision-making outcomes, whether an Article 6(3) condition is met, and whether the system performs profiling.

### Why

Under Annex III, point 4(a), high-risk AI systems include those intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, particularly to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates. The submitted system reads incoming CVs, discards applications lacking a driving licence (filtering), and outputs a ranked list of candidates to human recruiters (evaluating candidates).

Pursuant to Article 6(2), systems listed in Annex III are considered high-risk unless the derogation in Article 6(3) applies. Article 6(3) provides that an Annex III system is not high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, provided it meets at least one condition in Article 6(3), second subparagraph. 

Application of this derogation remains dependent on unresolved facts:
- Discarding applications without a driving licence automatically excludes individuals from human recruiter review, which could materially influence recruitment decisions unless established as a narrow procedural or preparatory filter.
- Generating a ranked list evaluates applicants, and although recruiters may interview anyone on the list, the influence of that ranking on human decision-making is unknown.
- Article 6(3), third subparagraph, establishes that an Annex III system is always high-risk if it performs profiling. The submission does not provide enough technical detail to determine whether the ranking process constitutes profiling.

### What could change this

The classification would shift to non-high-risk if it is established that:
- The system satisfies one of the criteria in Article 6(3), second subparagraph (such as performing a narrow procedural task or preparatory task);
- It does not materially influence decision outcomes or pose a significant risk to fundamental rights; and
- It does not perform profiling of natural persons.

If an Article 6(3) exception applies, the provider remains subject to documentation duties under Article 6(4).

### Missing facts

- The algorithm and criteria used to rank remaining candidates.
- Whether the candidate ranking involves profiling of natural persons.
- How recruiters interact with the ranked list in practice and the practical effect of the ranking on candidate selection.
- Whether rejected applications without a driving licence receive any human oversight.

### Timing and scope

This reading is provisional and limited strictly to the classification subset of Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113, the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026. However, pursuant to Article 113, point (c)(i), Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3—with the exception of Article 6(5)—apply from 2 December 2027 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III.

answer:
### Provisional finding
The AI system is provisionally classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 4, unless the provider demonstrates and documents that the derogation in Article 6(3) applies.

### Why
Under Article 6(2), AI systems listed in Annex III are considered high-risk. Annex III, point 4(a) encompasses AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to "analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates". 

The logistics company uses the system to filter incoming applications by automatically discarding those without a driving licence and to evaluate the remaining candidates by placing them into a ranked list for human recruiters. Because these functions fall directly within the recruitment use cases described in Annex III, point 4(a), the system meets the initial conditions for high-risk classification.

### What could change this
Under Article 6(3), an AI system referred to in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it "does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making", provided it satisfies one of four criteria (such as performing a narrow procedural task or a preparatory task to an assessment). 

However, Article 6(3) explicitly provides that an AI system "shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons". If the system carries out profiling or if its ranking materially influences the recruiters' selection outcomes, an Article 6(3) derogation cannot be established. If a provider relies on Article 6(3), it must fulfill the documentation and registration requirements set out in Article 6(4).

### Missing facts
- The specific technical criteria and algorithms used to rank candidates, including whether the system evaluates personal traits or undertakes profiling.
- The degree of reliance by recruiters: although recruiters may interview anyone on the list, it is not established whether the ranking in practice materially steers or predetermines interview invitations.
- Whether the provider has formally conducted, documented, and registered an assessment pursuant to Article 6(4).

### Timing and scope
This assessment is strictly limited to the classification provisions of Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113, the Regulation generally applies from 2 August 2026. However, under Article 113(c)(i), Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3—with the exception of Article 6(5)—apply from 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III.

Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities or on their behalf to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities as polygraphs or similar tools; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in support of law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of the investigation or prosecution of criminal offences; (d) AI systems intended to be used by law enforcement authorities or on their behalf or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, or to assess personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups; (e) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 in the course of the detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III — High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
retrieved_evidence.text: ANNEX III High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) High-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) are the AI systems listed in any of the following areas: 1. Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) remote biometric identification systems. This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be; (b) AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation, according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics; (c) AI systems intended to be used for emotion recognition. 2. Critical infrastructure: AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. 3. Education and vocational training: (a) AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (c) AI systems intended to be used for the purpose of assessing the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (d) AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. 4. Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. 5. Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits: (a) AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud; (c) AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance; (d) AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems. 6. Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities or on their behalf to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities as polygraphs or similar tools; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in support of law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of the investigation or prosecution of criminal offences; (d) AI systems intended to be used by law enforcement authorities or on their behalf or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, or to assess personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups; (e) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 in the course of the detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. 7. Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies as polygraphs or similar tools; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assist competent public authorities for the examination of applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and for associated complaints with regard to the eligibility of the natural persons applying for a status, including related assessments of the reliability of evidence; (d) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in the context of migration, asylum or border control management, for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, with the exception of the verification of travel documents. 8. Administration of justice and democratic processes: (a) AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority or on their behalf to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used in a similar way in alternative dispute resolution; (b) AI systems intended to be used for influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda. retrieved_evidence.label: Article 6 — Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems 1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; (b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. ▼M1 1a. For the purposes of this Regulation, including paragraph 1 of this Article, AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components. 1b. Notwithstanding paragraph 1a, AI systems the failure or malfunctioning of which would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components. 1c. A product that is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than risks to health and safety, in particular risks relating to the distribution of radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, shall not be considered as fulfilling the condition in paragraph 1, point (b). ▼B 2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. 3. By derogation from paragraph 2, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. The first subparagraph shall apply where any of the following conditions is fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III. Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons. 4. A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2). Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider shall provide the documentation of the assessment. 5. The Commission shall, after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board (the ‘Board’), and no later than 2 February 2026, provide guidelines specifying the practical implementation of this Article in line with Article 96 together with a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk. 6. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by adding new conditions to those laid down therein, or by modifying them, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of the existence of AI systems that fall under the scope of Annex III, but do not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. 7. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by deleting any of the conditions laid down therein, where there is concrete and reliable evidence that this is necessary to maintain the level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation. 8. Any amendment to the conditions laid down in paragraph 3, second subparagraph, adopted in accordance with paragraphs 6 and 7 of this Article shall not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation and shall ensure consistency with the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Article 7(1), and take account of market and technological developments.

retrieved_evidence.text: Article 113 Entry into force and application This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: ▼M1 (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025, with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026; ▼B (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; ▼M1 (c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I; ▼M1 (d) Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026. ▼B

answer:
### Provisional finding

The software provisionally falls under the high-risk education use cases in Annex III, point 3, which are subject to Article 6(2). However, whether the system is ultimately classified as high-risk or qualifies for the derogation in Article 6(3) depends on unresolved material facts: specifically, whether the software performs profiling and whether it materially influences the final evaluation rather than serving as a purely preparatory assessment.

### Why

Annex III, point 3(b) covers AI systems intended to be used:
> to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels

Annex III, point 3(c) also covers systems used to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or access. Scoring recorded oral examinations and suggesting a CEFR level within an educational institution directly relates to these use cases. Pursuant to Article 6(2), systems falling under Annex III are considered high-risk.

Under Article 6(3), an AI system referred to in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it:
> does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making

and satisfies one of the conditions in Article 6(3), such as performing a preparatory task to an assessment under Article 6(3)(d). While a teacher can change the level before it reaches the student, the mere possibility of human intervention does not resolve whether the software materially influences the decision. If teachers routinely defer to the suggested CEFR level without an independent substantive review, material influence may remain. In addition, Article 6(3) provides that any system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk.

### What could change this

- If the software performs profiling, the Article 6(3) exception cannot apply, confirming high-risk status under Article 6(2).
- If the provider demonstrates and documents under Article 6(4) that the system fulfills a condition under Article 6(3)—such as performing a preparatory task under Article 6(3)(d) without materially influencing the outcome—it would not be considered high-risk.
- If the tool is used outside formal educational assessment or institutional placement, Annex III, point 3 may not apply.

### Missing facts

- How teachers review the scores in practice, including whether they independently re-listen to the recordings or rely on the suggested output.
- Whether the system carries out profiling or analyzes student behavior beyond scoring oral responses.
- The institutional purpose and legal effect of the CEFR score (for example, course completion, admission, or formal certification).

### Timing and scope

This reading is provisional and strictly limited to the pinned classification subset: Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113(c)(i), high-risk rules for AI systems classified pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III apply from 2 December 2027, following the general application date of 2 August 2026 (subject to specific exceptions in Article 113, including Article 6(5)).

answer:
### Provisional finding

The software provisionally qualifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 3, subject to whether it satisfies the derogation conditions set out in Article 6(3).

### Why

Annex III, point 3(b) covers AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. By scoring recorded oral exams and generating CEFR proficiency levels, the software performs an automated evaluation of student educational performance. In addition, if the assigned CEFR level determines course placement or advancement, it may engage Annex III, point 3(c), which covers systems used to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or access. 

Under Article 6(2), systems falling within Annex III are high-risk. Although a teacher retains the ability to modify the suggested level before it reaches the student, human involvement does not automatically remove high-risk status. Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is exempt only if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and meets one of the conditions in Article 6(3)(a)–(d) (such as performing a preparatory task).

### What could change this

The classification would shift away from high-risk if:
- The system meets the conditions of Article 6(3)—for example, by serving as a purely preparatory aid under Article 6(3)(d) that does not materially influence the teacher's ultimate evaluation, provided the system does not perform profiling. If this derogation is claimed, the provider must document the assessment and comply with registration obligations under Article 6(4).
- The language school does not legally constitute an educational or vocational training institution within the meaning of Annex III, point 3.

Conversely, high-risk status would be confirmed without possibility of an Article 6(3) exception if the system performs profiling of natural persons, as Article 6(3) specifies that systems performing profiling shall always be considered high-risk.

### Missing facts

- Whether the private language school is recognized as an educational or vocational training institution.
- The actual workflow and extent of human review in practice, specifically whether teachers carry out an independent assessment of the recording or routinely defer to the suggested score.
- The downstream effect of the CEFR score (for example, internal practice feedback versus formal accredited certification or access to subsequent educational levels).
- Whether the system carries out profiling.

### Timing and scope

This provisional reading is based exclusively on the pinned subset consisting of Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113(c)(i), the requirements for high-risk AI systems classified pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III apply from 2 December 2027, with the exception of Article 6(5). Under Article 6(5), Commission guidelines specifying practical implementation and high-risk use cases are due no later than 2 February 2026.

retrieved_evidence.label: Article 6 — Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems 1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; (b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. ▼M1 1a. For the purposes of this Regulation, including paragraph 1 of this Article, AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components. 1b. Notwithstanding paragraph 1a, AI systems the failure or malfunctioning of which would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components. 1c. A product that is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than risks to health and safety, in particular risks relating to the distribution of radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, shall not be considered as fulfilling the condition in paragraph 1, point (b). ▼B 2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. 3. By derogation from paragraph 2, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. The first subparagraph shall apply where any of the following conditions is fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III. Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons. 4. A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2). Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider shall provide the documentation of the assessment. 5. The Commission shall, after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board (the ‘Board’), and no later than 2 February 2026, provide guidelines specifying the practical implementation of this Article in line with Article 96 together with a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk. 6. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by adding new conditions to those laid down therein, or by modifying them, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of the existence of AI systems that fall under the scope of Annex III, but do not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. 7. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by deleting any of the conditions laid down therein, where there is concrete and reliable evidence that this is necessary to maintain the level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation. 8. Any amendment to the conditions laid down in paragraph 3, second subparagraph, adopted in accordance with paragraphs 6 and 7 of this Article shall not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation and shall ensure consistency with the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Article 7(1), and take account of market and technological developments.

It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: ▼M1 (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025, with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026; ▼B (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; ▼M1 (c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I; ▼M1 (d) Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026. ▼B

answer:
### Provisional finding

The system provisionally qualifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(b), because it is used to evaluate the creditworthiness or risk profile of consumer loan applicants. A derogation under Article 6(3) is provisionally unavailable because the model materially influences credit decisions, though this classification depends on unresolved facts regarding whether the tool is strictly confined to fraud detection or whether it conducts profiling of natural persons.

### Why

Annex III, point 5(b) covers AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, exempting only those AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud. The system evaluates applicant bank-transaction summaries to generate an internal risk band and an actionable decision recommendation.

Under Article 6(2), systems falling within Annex III are classified as high-risk. Article 6(3) provides a derogation where a system does not pose a significant risk of harm, “including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making”, provided it meets one of four conditions in Article 6(3)(a)–(d). Because branch personnel “almost always follow” the recommendation, the system materially influences whether credit is granted, referred, or declined. Consequently, it fails the threshold criterion for the Article 6(3) derogation. Furthermore, Article 6(3) establishes that an Annex III system “shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons”.

### What could change this

- If factual evidence demonstrates that the model is used exclusively for detecting financial fraud, it would be excluded from high-risk classification under the express carve-out in Annex III, point 5(b).
- If the lender restructures workflow procedures so that the AI output does not materially influence the lending outcome, satisfies one of the specific conditions in Article 6(3)(a)–(d), and does not perform profiling, the provider could document an assessment that the system is not high-risk pursuant to Article 6(4).

### Missing facts

- Whether the transaction-summary model serves solely to detect fraud or evaluates broader applicant default risk and financial eligibility.
- Whether the model’s automated evaluation of applicant financial behavior constitutes profiling of natural persons.
- The degree of actual discretion exercised by branch staff, including why recommendations are followed almost uniformly and whether an independent, substantive human credit assessment occurs.

### Timing and scope

This assessment is a provisional reading against the classification subset comprising Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113, the Regulation generally applies from 2 August 2026. Pursuant to Article 113(c)(i), requirements for systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III apply from 2 December 2027, with the exception of Article 6(5), which requires Commission implementation guidelines no later than 2 February 2026.

### Provisional finding

The system provisionally qualifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6 and Annex III, point 5.

### Why

The submitted description states that a consumer lender uses a model to evaluate bank-transaction summaries, assign internal risk bands to loan applicants, and generate a “proceed / refer / decline” recommendation that branch staff almost always follow. 

Under Annex III, point 5, high-risk systems include:
> "AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud;"

Pursuant to Article 6, systems listed in Annex III are classified as high-risk. Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system may derogate from high-risk classification if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and meets one of the four specific conditions in points (a) to (d). Because branch staff almost always follow the system's recommendations, the output appears to directly affect the lending outcome. In addition, Article 6(3) explicitly provides that an Annex III system always remains high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

### What could change this

- **Fraud detection carve-out**: If the system is used solely for detecting financial fraud rather than assessing creditworthiness, it would fall under the express exclusion in Annex III, point 5.
- **Article 6(3) derogation**: The classification could change if the provider demonstrates that the system does not pose a significant risk of harm, does not materially influence decisions, satisfies one of the conditions in Article 6(3)(a)–(d), and does not perform profiling of natural persons. 
- **Documentation duties**: If relying on an Article 6(3) exception, the provider must document its assessment prior to putting the system into service pursuant to Article 6(4).

### Missing facts

- Whether the system's purpose includes or is restricted to the detection of financial fraud.
- The exact decision-making protocol and whether staff exercise substantive, independent evaluation beyond the model's output.
- Whether the transaction-summary analysis constitutes profiling of natural persons under applicable rules.
- Whether the provider has documented a non-high-risk assessment under Article 6(4).

### Timing and scope

This provisional reading is limited solely to the classification subset comprising Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113, the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026; however, pursuant to Article 113(c)(i), Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3 (with the exception of Article 6(5)) apply from 2 December 2027 for systems classified under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III, point 1
retrieved_evidence.text: 1. Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) remote biometric identification systems. This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be; (b) AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation, according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics; (c) AI systems intended to be used for emotion recognition.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III, point 7
retrieved_evidence.text: 7. Migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies as polygraphs or similar tools; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assist competent public authorities for the examination of applications for asylum, visa or residence permits and for associated complaints with regard to the eligibility of the natural persons applying for a status, including related assessments of the reliability of evidence; (d) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in the context of migration, asylum or border control management, for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, with the exception of the verification of travel documents.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III, point 8
retrieved_evidence.text: 8. Administration of justice and democratic processes: (a) AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority or on their behalf to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used in a similar way in alternative dispute resolution; (b) AI systems intended to be used for influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda. This does not include AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

retrieved_evidence.label: Article 6(1)
retrieved_evidence.text: 1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; (b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I.

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III, point 2

retrieved_evidence.label: Annex III — High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
retrieved_evidence.text: ANNEX III High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) High-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) are the AI systems listed in any of the following areas: 1. Biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) remote biometric identification systems. This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be; (b) AI systems intended to be used for biometric categorisation, according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics; (c) AI systems intended to be used for emotion recognition. 2. Critical infrastructure: AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. 3. Education and vocational training: (a) AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (c) AI systems intended to be used for the purpose of assessing the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels; (d) AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. 4. Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships. 5. Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits: (a) AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services; (b) AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud; (c) AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance; (d) AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems. 6. Law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law: (a) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities or on their behalf to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences; (b) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities as polygraphs or similar tools; (c) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in support of law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of the investigation or prosecution of criminal offences; (d) AI systems intended to be used by law enforcement authorities or on their behalf or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, or to assess personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups; (e) AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of law enforcement authorities for the profiling of natural persons as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 in the course of the detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. 7. retrieved_evidence.label: Article 6 — Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems 1. Irrespective of whether an AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the products referred to in points (a) and (b), that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; (b) the product whose safety component pursuant to point (a) is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. ▼M1 1a. For the purposes of this Regulation, including paragraph 1 of this Article, AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components. 1b. Notwithstanding paragraph 1a, AI systems the failure or malfunctioning of which would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components. 1c. A product that is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than risks to health and safety, in particular risks relating to the distribution of radio spectrum or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, shall not be considered as fulfilling the condition in paragraph 1, point (b). ▼B 2. In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. 3. By derogation from paragraph 2, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. The first subparagraph shall apply where any of the following conditions is fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review; or (d) the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the purposes of the use cases listed in Annex III. Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons. 4. A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2). Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider shall provide the documentation of the assessment. 5. The Commission shall, after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board (the ‘Board’), and no later than 2 February 2026, provide guidelines specifying the practical implementation of this Article in line with Article 96 together with a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk. 6. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by adding new conditions to those laid down therein, or by modifying them, where there is concrete and reliable evidence of the existence of AI systems that fall under the scope of Annex III, but do not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons. 7. The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by deleting any of the conditions laid down therein, where there is concrete and reliable evidence that this is necessary to maintain the level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation. 8. Any amendment to the conditions laid down in paragraph 3, second subparagraph, adopted in accordance with paragraphs 6 and 7 of this Article shall not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided for by this Regulation and shall ensure consistency with the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Article 7(1), and take account of market and technological developments.

retrieved_evidence.label: Article 113 — Entry into force and application
retrieved_evidence.text: Article 113 Entry into force and application This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: ▼M1 (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025, with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026; ▼B (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; ▼M1 (c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I; ▼M1 (d) Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026. ▼B

answer:
### Provisional finding

The system provisionally classifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 1(a). This finding depends on two unresolved material facts: whether the turnstile entry process operates purely as 1-to-many remote biometric identification rather than 1-to-1 biometric verification of a prior identity claim, and whether its deployment is permitted under relevant Union or national law.

### Why

Annex III, point 1 covers biometrics "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law". Specifically, Annex III, point 1(a) classifies "remote biometric identification systems" as high-risk. Point 1(a) explicitly provides: "This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be". 

Based on the stated facts, lobby cameras scan faces and compare them against an entire employee watchlist to grant access or flag security. Because the described setup searches across a database rather than verifying an identity claimed by the person (such as presenting an ID badge first), it functions as a 1-to-many biometric identification system rather than verification. Consequently, if legally permitted under applicable law, it falls within Annex III, point 1(a) and is high-risk under Article 6(2).

An exception under Article 6(3) is unlikely to succeed because the software autonomously controls gate access and dispatches security on mismatches, directly and materially influencing physical access decisions. Furthermore, if a provider were to claim an Article 6(3) derogation, it would still have to document its assessment before deployment and register the system pursuant to Article 6(4).

### What could change this

- **Existence of an identity claim:** If individuals present an access card or input a credential prior to image capture, the software may serve solely to confirm that the person is the individual they claim to be, exempting it under Annex III, point 1(a).
- **Legality under Union or national law:** If the biometric processing is not legally permitted under applicable Union or national data protection and labour laws, it does not satisfy the threshold condition of Annex III, point 1.
- **Article 6(3) documentation:** High-risk status would not apply if the provider documents under Article 6(4) that the system fulfills one of the conditions in Article 6(3) and poses no significant risk of harm, provided it does not perform profiling.

### Missing facts

- Whether entrants present a card, PIN, or other identity claim prior to camera comparison.
- Whether the system is legally permitted under applicable Union or national law.
- Whether the system performs profiling of natural persons.

### Timing and scope

This assessment is strictly provisional and confined to the pinned classification subset of Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. Under Article 113, the Regulation applies generally from 2 August 2026. However, under Article 113(c)(i), Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3—with the exception of Article 6(5)—apply from 2 December 2027 to AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III.

answer:
### Provisional finding

The lobby turnstile facial comparison system provisionally falls within the scope of a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 1(a), unless it qualifies as a biometric verification system or meets the derogation conditions set out in Article 6(3).

### Why

- AI systems listed in Annex III are classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2).
- Annex III, point 1 addresses biometrics, "in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law", and covers in point 1(a) "remote biometric identification systems."
- The submitted facts indicate that cameras scan individuals at turnstiles and compare faces against an "employee watchlist" to trigger gate opening or staff alerts. Comparing facial biometrics against a watchlist constitutes a one-to-many identification function.
- Annex III, point 1(a) explicitly excludes certain verification systems: "This shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be". Because the system checks persons against a collective watchlist without an individual claim of identity, it falls under remote biometric identification rather than the verification exception.

### What could change this

- **Biometric verification carve-out**: If the architecture requires users to claim an identity first (for instance, by presenting an access badge or entering a credential) and the facial analysis is used exclusively to confirm that the user is indeed that specific individual, the system would meet the exclusion in Annex III, point 1(a) and fall outside that high-risk classification.
- **Article 6(3) derogation**: Under Article 6(3), an AI system referred to in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, provided it meets one of the specific conditions in Article 6(3) (such as performing a narrow procedural task). However, under Article 6(3), the system is always considered high-risk if it performs profiling.
- **Provider documentation**: A provider seeking to rely on Article 6(3) must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, in accordance with Article 6(4).
- **Article 6(1) classification**: If the turnstile gate mechanism or software constitutes a safety component of a product governed by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and requires a third-party conformity assessment pursuant to Article 6(1), it could be classified as high-risk independently of Annex III.

### Missing facts

- **Claim of identity**: Whether the system identifies users purely from camera feeds against a watchlist (one-to-many), or verifies a specific claimed identity initiated by a card or token (one-to-one).
- **Profiling**: Whether the system conducts any profiling of employees or visitors.
- **Capture setup**: The operational parameters of the lobby cameras (for example, whether capture occurs at a distance without user cooperation).
- **Article 6(4) assessment**: Whether the provider has formally documented an evaluation asserting that the system does not pose a significant risk under Article 6(3).
- **Legal permissibility**: Whether the biometric processing is permitted under applicable Union or national law, as referenced in Annex III, point 1.

### Timing and scope

This provisional finding is restricted exclusively to the pinned classification subset comprising Article 6, Annex III, and Article 113. It does not determine full regulatory compliance, conformity assessment status, or whether the system is subject to prohibitions under other parts of the EU AI Act.

Pursuant to Article 113, the Regulation applies generally from 2 August 2026. However, under Article 113(c)(i), Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3—with the exception of Article 6(5)—apply from 2 December 2027 to AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III. AI systems classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) apply from 2 August 2028 pursuant to Article 113(c)(ii).

answer:
### Provisional finding

The submitted AI system is provisionally not classified as a high-risk AI system under the assessed classification framework.

### Why

The classification of an AI system as high-risk under this framework depends on whether it satisfies the product safety criteria in Article 6(1) or falls within any of the designated use cases in Annex III pursuant to Article 6(2).

1. **Article 6(1) evaluation**: Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Under Article 6(1a), systems used solely for non-safety aspects such as customer assistance, automation, or convenience do not qualify as safety components. An informational customer service chatbot for furniture delivery and returns is not a safety component and does not fall under Annex I.
2. **Article 6(2) and Annex III evaluation**: Annex III enumerates specific high-risk application areas: biometrics (Annex III, point 1), critical infrastructure (Annex III, point 2), education and vocational training (Annex III, point 3), employment and worker management (Annex III, point 4), access to essential private and public services (Annex III, point 5), law enforcement (Annex III, point 6), migration and border control (Annex III, point 7), and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, point 8). Providing FAQ responses on retail delivery timelines and return policies does not meet any of these descriptors. It does not evaluate creditworthiness or insurance risk (Annex III, point 5), nor does it perform dispute resolution on behalf of judicial bodies (Annex III, point 8).
3. **Article 6(3) derogation and Article 6(4)**: Because the chatbot does not fall under any Annex III category, the derogation assessment under Article 6(3) and the documentation and registration requirements under Article 6(4) are not triggered.

### What could change this

The classification would change if the system's intended purpose or functional scope were modified to intersect with high-risk categories:
- If the chatbot were expanded to evaluate customer creditworthiness or eligibility for financing purchases (Annex III, point 5(b)).
- If it were deployed to conduct biometric identification, biometric categorisation, or emotion recognition on website visitors (Annex III, point 1).
- If it were integrated into a product governed by Annex I legislation where its failure could endanger health and safety (Article 6(1b)).

### Missing facts

- Whether the chatbot processes personal data or engages in automated profiling beyond standard FAQ retrieval.
- Whether there are unstated operational integrations, such as automated handling of legal claims, payment handling, or fraud scoring.

### Timing and scope

This reading is strictly provisional and limited to the classification rules in Article 6, Annex III, and the temporal applicability rules in Article 113. It does not constitute a full regulatory conformity review and does not evaluate obligations outside this subset, such as transparency duties for systems interacting with natural persons.

Under Article 113, the Regulation generally applies from 2 August 2026. For systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3 apply from 2 December 2027 under Article 113(c)(i), while systems classified under Article 6(1) and Annex I apply from 2 August 2028 under Article 113(c)(ii). Commission guidelines under Article 6(5) are scheduled by 2 February 2026.
